label: Shot size
description: Named shot sizes, portrait crops, subject groupings, and selfie framings.
notes: Framing extent, named portrait crops, subject groupings, and selfie setups belong here, phrased as named shots with an article. Chest-up and medium close-up share one entry; three-quarter shot means a knee-up crop here, while cowboy shot ends at mid-thigh. camera.angle owns independently chosen camera height, direction, and tilt; the profile portrait is retained as a familiar named framing. camera.lens owns lens effects, and camera.film_look owns film and format looks. Pose, expression, and lighting belong in their own lists rather than being bundled into framing variants.

values.look: A tiny feature, such as one eye or a mouth, fills the frame; the rest of the subject is cut off.
The face or main subject fills nearly the entire frame, with little background visible.
The entire head and the tops of both shoulders show, with the crop near the collarbone.
A close side view of the head shows one eye and the outline of the forehead, nose, lips, and chin.
One small part of a larger subject fills the image, such as stitching on a coat or a carved door handle.
The head, shoulders, and upper chest show; the frame ends around the middle of the chest.
The person is framed from the waist up, leaving room for arms, hands, and some background.
The person is framed from the head to mid-thigh, keeping the hips and hands beside them visible.
Only the body between the neck and waist is visible; the head and legs fall outside the frame.
The person is visible from the head to around the knees, with the lower legs and feet outside the frame.
The entire person is visible from head to feet and occupies most of the frame height.
The whole subject is visible with ample space around it, making the surrounding setting easy to read.
The setting dominates the image; any person is a tiny figure within a much larger landscape or space.
A broad view identifies the location, showing a building or landscape together with its immediate surroundings.
A person shares the frame with their workspace or everyday setting, including objects that show what they do there.
An extra-wide horizontal frame stretches across the scene, taking in far more from side to side than top to bottom.
Two people share the frame with comparable prominence, so their relationship and interaction are visible.
The back of one person’s head and shoulder edges the foreground while another person faces them beyond.
The photographer’s face and shoulders fill the near foreground, often with an outstretched arm entering an edge.
A mirror reflection shows the photographer from the waist up, with the phone visible in one hand.
A tall mirror shows the photographer’s entire body and outfit, with the phone visible in the reflection.
Several faces crowd close to the camera, with the person holding it nearest the foreground.
A specific object or action fills the frame, such as a key in a lock or fingers pressing a button.
The scene appears through a participant’s eyes, often with their hands or feet entering the bottom of the frame.
Three or more people are arranged together so each person’s face is clearly visible within the shared frame.
The person occupies one edge or corner, leaving most of the frame as a plain wall, sky, or other empty area.
A doorway, window, arch, or other foreground opening forms a visible border around the subject.
The person is seen in a mirror or window reflection, with the reflective surface or its edges visible.
